blueprint_topic: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies — insulin pump interruption safety
stem: A client with type 1 diabetes uses an insulin pump. Which teaching point is most important regarding interruption of pump insulin delivery?

options.A: Because pumps provide rapid- or ultra-rapid-acting insulin continuously, interruption can allow ketosis or diabetic ketoacidosis to develop rapidly, so the client should follow the prescribed troubleshooting and backup plan promptly.
options.B: A pump interruption can generally be ignored for about a day because a depot of long-acting insulin remains under the skin and continues to provide basal insulin during device failure.
options.C: Pump therapy removes the need to monitor glucose during delivery problems because automated insulin systems continue to prevent dangerous hyperglycemia even when insulin flow is interrupted.
options.D: When pump delivery stops, the client should avoid backup insulin until the pump is professionally repaired because supplemental insulin increases the risk of ketosis during an interruption.

rationale: ADA Standards of Care in Diabetes—2026 describe insulin pumps as delivering rapid-acting insulin throughout the day; the 2026 pharmacologic treatment table lists rapid development of ketosis or diabetic ketoacidosis with interruption of insulin delivery as a disadvantage of pump therapy. Thus an interruption requires prompt recognition and use of the person's prescribed troubleshooting and backup plan. Therefore A is correct. B falsely assumes a long-acting insulin depot, C incorrectly removes the need for monitoring, and D recommends withholding needed backup insulin.
educational_objective: Teach insulin-pump users that interruption of rapid- or ultra-rapid-acting insulin delivery can rapidly lead to ketosis or diabetic ketoacidosis and requires prompt use of the prescribed troubleshooting and backup plan.
source_document_title: 7. Diabetes Technology: Standards of Care in Diabetes—2026; 9. Pharmacologic Approaches to Glycemic Treatment: Standards of Care in Diabetes—2026
source_version_date: Standards of Care in Diabetes—2026, Diabetes Care 49(Suppl. 1), published 2026; accessed 2026-08-26
source_locator: Section 7 > Stand-alone Insulin Pumps and AID Systems: pumps deliver rapid-acting insulin throughout the day. Section 9 > insulin pump therapy table: basal delivery of ultra-rapid/rapid-acting insulin; disadvantage is risk of rapid development of ketosis or DKA with interruption of insulin delivery.
source_claim_supported: Insulin pumps deliver rapid- or ultra-rapid-acting insulin, and interruption of delivery carries a risk of rapid development of ketosis or DKA.
blueprint_locator: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies, printed p.12/PDF p.16: administer medications safely; educate clients about medications and delivery technology; recognize and respond to medication-therapy complications.
candidate_reasons_resolved: Rewrote all four choices as substantive pump-interruption safety statements without absolute-word distractor cues.
Balanced option length and retained the exact ADA 2026 risk statement without inventing a universal time-to-DKA interval.
audit_note: Independent adversarial review confirms A uniquely matches ADA 2026 pump-safety guidance. The item avoids unsupported numeric timing and makes the required response depend on the prescribed backup/troubleshooting plan rather than a fabricated universal protocol.
